ABSTRACT
An integrative solid oxide fuel cell combined cooling, heating and power system in green buildings with
hydrogen energy of byproduct water enables carbon neutrality transformation. However, underlying mecha-
nisms on capacity sizing of combined cooling, heating and power system devices and its impacts on system
techno-economy have not been figured out especially considering dynamic degradation and efficiency of asso-
ciated devices. In this study, a multi-software optimization platform is established by MATLAB-TRNSYS co-
simulation for sizing parametrical analysis, with well balance of modelling complexity and computational effi-
ciency. A self-sufficient combined cooling, heating and power system is modelled integrating with a semi-
empirical surrogate model of solid oxide fuel cell to interact with other balance of plant types efficiently.
Total energy efficiency and annual total cost are optimized through parametrical analysis on device size of each
component (battery, electrolyzer and solid oxide fuel cell) and analysis of variance for contribution ratio
quantification. Results indicate that, the size increase in electrolyzer and solid oxide fuel cell will improve system
total energy efficiency by 13.635 % and 2.194 %, but promote annual total cost by 4.042 × 10

1. Introduction
As a common pursuit of carbon neutrality target around the world
[1] , hydrogen energy has experienced substantial growth in both in-
dustrial sectors and academic circles in recent years [2] , due to its
prominent merits of extreme clean [3] , high enthalpy [4] , carbon free
and easy long-term storage [5] . Solid oxide fuel cell (SOFC) has been
attracted increasing attention because of its ability to convert hydrogen
into heat and electricity with high-quality heat. SOFC stack consists of
series of cells containing interconnected bipolar plate, anode and cath-
ode electrodes, and electrolyte for transporting ions. Wherein hydrogen
will be oxidized and release electrons in anode. The released electrons
will be transported into cathode by outside circuit, and reduce oxygen
into ions in cathode. Afterwards, the oxygen ions will be transported to
anode across the electrolyte, and combined with hydrogen ions to
generate water. There are several types of SOFC, such as samarium-
doped ceria (SDC) and yttria stabilized zirconia (YSZ) for electrolyte

The SOFC has been applied in combined heating and power (CHP)
system or combined cooling, heating and power (CCHP) system to cover
the daily energy demands of buildings, contributing significantly to
carbon neutrality transformation in green buildings [8] . The CCHP/CHP
system will be integrated with other devices to adapt to variable sce-
narios, such as photovoltaic (PV) panel [9] , battery [10] and electro-
lyzer [11] , for long-time standalone operations. Those key device sizes,
i.e., the cell number of the battery, electrolyzer, SOFC and etc., play a
significant role in system economic feasibility and energy efficiency.
Modeling analysis is an effective way to investigate the device size ef-
fects, with attributes of high efficiency and cost saving compared to in-
field experiments [12] . By relying on computational simulation, it is
necessary to guarantee the detailed information of integrated
components and calculation efficiency of the CCHP/CHP system
modeling for overall performance analysis.
Besides, the capacity size of key devices will determine the invest-
ment cost of the CCHP/CHP system [13] , and affect the system economic
efficiency and implementation feasibility. On the other hand, the depth
of discharge (DOD) and service lifetime (like battery and SOFC) will also
be dependent on their sizes [14] . Therefore, it is necessary to design
appropriate sizes of key devices to avoid performance overestimation
and improve techno-economic feasibility.
Optimization analysis is an effective way to identify the optimal
designs of CCHP/CHP systems, including operating control [15] , ma-
terial selection [16] and structure size [17] . High-dimensional modeling
is usually used for device performance analysis and figuring out the
system detailed characteristics by optimization. Pang et al. [18] opti-
mized a steam ejector applied in a CHP system by comparing three
design cases, through the finite element modeling and computational
fluid dynamics analysis in Fluent software, which will consume a large
amount of time for device performance calculation. They found that the

ejector designed with the optimized thermodynamic method possessed
higher heat recovery efficiency. Gao et al. [19] proposed a cross-scale
model of CHP system and established a fuel cell device model by
computational fluid dynamics analysis in Fluent software, aiming to
improve the fuel cell model accuracy. It is distinct that detailed
modeling in high-dimensional is time-consuming for calculation because
it needs to be solved by nonlinearly iterative calculation based on
gradient descent method in each boundary condition solving, not to
mention the global optimization by algorithm. While in order to achieve
high-efficiency global optimization, the system devices are usually
established in zero dimension, such as physical model or machine
learning model. Yuan et al. [20] optimized a CHP system energy effi-
ciency based on an artificial neural network model of input operating
parameters and output efficiency relationship through the genetic al-
gorithm calculation. The results showed that the system energy effi-
ciency reached 95.62 %. Liu et al. [21] developed a zero-dimensional
SOFC CCHP system model to analyze the thermal-economic perfor-
mance by multi-objective optimization. They found that the total energy
output and exergy efficiency could increase by 35.58 kW and 0.20 %,
respectively. Besides, some research also explores methods to balance
the calculation efficiency and model complexity. Darzi et al. [22] pro-
posed a partial high-dimensional modeling method to optimize the spark
plug location in CHP system, namely one-dimensional modeling of en-
gine and three-dimensional modeling of cold flow in engine space,
which can improve the calculation efficiency and guarantee the model
accuracy to some extent, whereas the calculation efficiency is still
limited. Obviously, high-dimensional model is hard to be applied in
long-time scenario simulation and optimization, and device modeling is
usually simplified to achieve a high-efficiency calculation in global
optimization, with sacrifice or simplification of the device detailed
characteristics. It is highly necessary to balance both model complexity
and computational efficiency in the multi-scale optimization.
Sizing analyses of CCHP/CHP systems have been conducted to
reduce total cost [23], improve energy saving [24], and reduce carbon
emission [25], etc. Liu et al. [25] analyzed the capacity of prime mover
in a CCHP system for optimal economic feasibility, and finally they
identified the best capacity of the prime mover at 78.146 kW. Shahsavari
et al. [26] analyzed the best energy cost of a CHP system in rural resi-
dential areas by sizing the system configuration, and they found that the
optimal cost could be achieved through the design of 39.4-kW PV, 10-
kW diesel generators, 20.1-kW converter, device number of 20 wind
turbines and 96 batteries. Benalcazar et al. [27] proposed a mixed-
integer linear programming approach to find the optimal capacity of a
CHP system thermal energy storage. They found that the integration of
thermal energy storage capacity would save the cost of € 0.57 M – € 0.64
M in Poland. Wang et al. [23] investigated the optimal size of equipment
in the photovoltaic/thermal (PV/T) panel CCHP system by a bi-level
optimization. The results indicate that the improvement of PV/T-
CCHP system size could save the annual total cost of 5.82 % and
reduce the carbon emission of 37.51 %. However, there are few studies
about SOFC CCHP/CHP system sizing, and the CCHP/CHP system per-
formance is highly dependent on the SOFC electrical/thermal efficiency,
while the impacts of SOFC size on the SOFC electrical/thermal efficiency
has been rarely discussed. Besides, the system sizing research has sel-
domly connected the device size design with its degradation perfor-
mance, and this ignorance will lead to inaccurate estimations on the
system lifetime and economic efficiency.
The collaborative sizing optimization of multiple devices in CCHP/
CHP system is able to improve the system performance comprehensively
[23]. Guo et al. [28] optimized the sizes of the proton exchange mem-
brane fuel cell (PEMFC) and auxiliary chiller in a CCHP system. It
indicated that the system energy efficiency could be improved by 23.21
%. Wang et al. [29] optimized the device capacity size of a CCHP system
by multi-objective optimization algorithm for optimal carbon emission
and economic cost. The results showed that the carbon emission and
economic cost have been reduced by 99.81 % and 66.70 % respectively
compared to single objective optimization. Shahsavari et al. [26] iden-
tified the power capacity of PV panels, diesel generator, and converter,
and installed number of wind turbines, battery and boiler in a CHP
system. The results indicate that the energy cost could be reduced by
34.8 % under the optimal identification. Nonetheless, few studies have
discussed the capacity sizing optimization of SOFC CCHP/CHP system.
In addition, the contribution ranks of different key devices on CCHP/
CHP system performances have not been figured out during the sizing
optimization, especially combining the impacts of dynamic degradation
condition and energy conversion efficiency.
Based on the above literature review, the research gaps can be
summarized as follows:
1) The global optimization analysis of SOFC CCHP system has usually
scarified or simplified the model complexity of detailed character-
istics to guarantee the computational efficiency in zero-dimensional
modeling, while the simplified model has limited the authenticity
and reliability of the CCHP system model. It is necessary to well
balance the model complexity and computational efficiency of the
CCHP system.
2) In the academia, studies are quite limited on the sizing analysis
regarding the integrative SOFC CCHP system, and the impact of
device size (like battery, electrolyzer and SOFC) on their degradation
performance has been usually ignored, resulting in inaccurate esti-
mation of the overall techno-economic performance. Besides, the
underlying mechanism of the SOFC size on the overall electrical/
thermal efficiency has been seldomly investigated. Furthermore,
sensitivity analysis of key device sizes on techno-economic perfor-
mances of the integrative SOFC CCHP system has not been figured
out.
3) In the academia, studies are quite limited on the size capacity opti-
mization of integrative SOFC CCHP system, and the optimal designs
of key device sizes to maximize techno-economic performances of
the integrative SOFC-CCHP system have not been investigated,
especially considering the dynamic degradation performance and
energy efficiency simultaneously.
Main contributions of this study are summarized below:
1) In order to well balance both model complexity and computational
efficiency of the integrative SOFC-CCHP system, a multi-software
optimization platform is established based on MATLAB-TRNSYS
co-simulation framework of a CCHP system coupling with a SOFC
semi-empirical surrogate model. This aims to enable the multi-
objective optimization with high computational efficiency and
model complexity.
2) In order to clearly demonstrate the significance of key device size
design (like battery, electrolyzer and SOFC) on the integrative SOFC-
CCHP system, the impact of key device size analyses has been con-
ducted on dynamic electrical/thermal efficiency and overall techno-
economic performance of the integrative SOFC-CCHP system (like
system energy efficiency, degradation level and annual cost), which
also considers dynamic degradation performance. Furthermore,
significance ranks of key device sizes on techno-economic perfor-
mances of the integrative SOFC-CCHP system are identified through
the analysis of variance (ANOVA) method, in terms of system total
energy efficiency and annual total cost.
3) Multi-objective optimization and posteriori multi-criteria decision
making on an integrative SOFC-CCHP system have been conducted.
The optimal size designs are selected by normalized Euclidean dis-
tance along the multi-objective Pareto front to identify the ‘best of
the best’ solution to maximize system total energy efficiency and
minimize annual total cost.
This study is organized as follows. Section 2 introduces the estab-
lishing process of the SOFC-CCHP system model based on multi-software

2.1. Multi-software optimization platform
Fig. 1 describes the framework design of the multi-software optimi-
zation platform, consisting of the cross callings between MATLAB and
TRNSYS. As for MATLAB-calling-TRNSYS, the non-dominated sorting
genetic algorithm II (NSGA-II) module in MATLAB will control the
TRNSYS-calling module to open TRNSYS and then activate the CCHP
system model running, and simultaneously input the independent var-
iables into the CCHP system model by interaction files. The CCHP system
model in TRNSYS is integrated with the residential building power de-
mands, which is based on the specific climate effects from Meteonorm
database. The control strategy is conducted on CCHP system during the
operation process for cost-effectiveness. The CCHP system performances
(such as energy efficiency, annual cost, etc) will be output back to NSGA-
II algorithm module in MATLAB by interaction files after finishing the
scenario operations. As for TRNSYS-calling-MATLAB, the CCHP system
model in TRNSYS has integrated with the SOFC model in MATLAB by
MATLAB-calling type, and drive the SOFC model calculating in each
time step during scenario operation. The operating conditions (inlet gas
pressure, temperature, species, load current, etc) will be input to the
SOFC theoretical model to calculate the SOFC performance, including
voltage, electrical power, thermal power, and etc. Afterwards, the fitting
coefficients of the SOFC semi-empirical model will be estimated based
on the load current and electrical/thermal power performances. The
estimated semi-empirical model of SOFC will then calculate the SOFC
stack performance corresponding to the variable load current, and
interact with other balance of plant (BOP) models for high-efficiency
response. When the operating boundary conditions (inlet gas pressure,
stoichiometric ratio, inlet gas fraction and inlet gas temperature) are
changed, the fitting coefficients of the semi-empirical model will be
updated by once fitting correspondingly.
The CCHP system operation is self-sufficient by only renewable en-
ergy support without power grid input, which can be applied in some
standalone scenarios, such as the building energy coverage in stand-
alone islands. The lithium iron phosphate (LFP) battery is adopted for
energy storage in CCHP system, due to its merits of low cost, high safety
and excellent thermal stability [30] . Besides, the proton exchange

2.2.3. Solid oxide fuel cell theoretical modeling
The cell number of SOFC affects the electrical/thermal energy effi-
ciency, as shown in Fig. 2 (a). Specifically, when the output electrical
power demand of SOFC stack is similar, each cell of SOFC stack will hold

lower overpotential, i.e., the higher electrical energy efficiency and
lower thermal energy efficiency. Besides, the performance degradation
will promote thermal energy efficiency, as shown in Fig. 2 (b). The SOFC
contains a lower cell voltage after degradation when covering a similar
electrical power demand, indicating that SOFC has a higher over-
potential with more heat production. Thus, the SOFC cell number and

Specifically, the DHW heating power demand is stable around the year.
The electrical power will be much higher during winter (0 – 1460 h,

kW. The space cooling power demand and space heating power demand

transient behaviors of the devices maintaining within 0.25 h will not be

2.3.2. Control strategy
The control strategy of the CCHP system has distinguished different
dominated power-supply devices (battery and SOFC) during daily
operation, and taking two days in winter and summer respectively for
instances, Fig. 4 illustrates the daily power demands of the residential
building and operation conditions of battery and SOFC. The peak power
demand period during the whole day will be covered by SOFC energy
supply, i.e., 6:00 am – 10:00 am and 17:00 pm – 2:00 am, and the valley
power demand period will be covered by battery energy supply,
including periods of 2:00 am – 6:00 am and 10:00 am – 17:00 am. Be-
sides, the start-up period of SOFC stack will be set as 2 h [42] (4:00 am –
6:00 am and 15:00 am – 17:00 am), during which the battery will supply
the BOP component operation and assist the SOFC stack to heat up from
the ambient temperature (non-working state) to setpoint temperature
(preparing-working state). The period-classified power supply by SOFC
and battery alternating domination is able to achieve more cost-effective
performance, due to the alternately intermittent rest of the power supply
devices, which can reduce by 11.83 % annual total cost compared to the
operation strategy of both battery (only BOP energy supply) and SOFC
(only building demand supply) working continuously without rest [32] .

4. Conclusions
In this study, a multi-software optimization platform is established
based on MATLAB-TRNSYS co-simulation framework for a CCHP system
key device sizing (i.e., battery, electrolyzer and SOFC). A SOFC semi-
empirical model is developed and integrated with the co-simulation
framework to substitute the SOFC stack for interacting with other BOP
models for high-efficiency response. The size effects of battery, elec-
trolyzer and SOFC are analyzed comprehensively on the system total
energy efficiency, device degradation level and annual total cost. Be-
sides, the optimal size designs of battery, electrolyzer and SOFC are
investigated by multi-objective optimization, considering optimal
annual total cost and total energy efficiency. Meanwhile, the contribu-
tion ratios of the key device sizes are identified on system techno-
economic performances by ANOVA analysis. The main results are
summarized as follows:
1) To well balance the modelling complexity and computational effi-
ciency CCHP system, the developed SOFC semi-empirical model is
highly accurate in both theoretical model surrogate and SOFC per-
formance prediction. The SOFC semi-empirical model can surrogate

The research results provide a new modeling method by integrating
with semi-empirical surrogate model to improve the co-simulation ef-
ficiency, and give a guidance for the CCHP system sizing for excellent
techno-economic feasibility. Besides, the contribution rank analysis
figures out the device significances in the CCHP system design. In
addition, the research work contributes to improving the widespread
application of hydrogen energy in buildings, and accelerates the
decarbonization process in communities, which will enable the carbon
neutrality in districts for extreme climate mitigation.
